DOCUMENT:
Internal Audit Memo: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy
To: Director of Operations, Therapies Division
From: Clinical Audit Team
Date: 14 August 2026

1. Scope
This audit examined missed appointments in the outpatient physiotherapy service across our three clinic sites between 1 January and 30 June 2026. For the purposes of this audit, a "did not attend" (DNA) is recorded when a patient fails to attend without giving notice. Late cancellations (less than 24 hours' notice) are recorded and reported separately, because the slot can sometimes be offered to another patient. We reviewed the appointment system records for all 24,860 booked appointments in the period and interviewed reception and clinical staff at each site.

2. Overall position
There were 2,610 DNAs in the period, a DNA rate of 10.5%, against the service target of 8%. Each DNA leaves a 30-minute clinical slot unused. At the service's average cost per clinical hour of £62, the 1,305 lost clinical hours represent around £80,900 of clinical time over six months.

Table 1. DNA rate by appointment type
Appointment type | Booked | DNAs | DNA rate
New patient assessment | 6,210 | 410 | 6.6%
Follow-up | 18,650 | 2,200 | 11.8%
Total | 24,860 | 2,610 | 10.5%

Follow-up appointments account for most DNAs. Staff told us that many patients stop attending once their symptoms improve, without telling the service.

3. Reminder calls
Since 2024, reception staff have phoned patients two working days before their appointment where time allows. In the audit period, staff made reminder calls for 7,800 appointments, about 300 a week over the 26 weeks. A call is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded. Reception staff estimate that each call, including dialling, rescheduling where needed and updating the record, takes an average of four minutes.

Table 2. DNA rate by reminder status
Reminder status | Appointments | DNAs | DNA rate
Reminder call received | 7,800 | 470 | 6.0%
No reminder call recorded | 17,060 | 2,140 | 12.5%

Patients who received a reminder call were less than half as likely to miss their appointment. Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate, and extending them to all appointments would bring the service well within its 8% target.

4. Discharge policy
The service's policy is that a patient who DNAs twice without explanation is discharged back to their referrer. We found the policy was applied inconsistently: of 160 patients who met the criterion, 104 were discharged. Staff were reluctant to discharge patients they knew to be vulnerable.

5. Late cancellations
In addition to the DNAs above, 1,140 appointments were cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice. Reception staff were able to refill 31% of these slots, usually with patients on the cancellation list.

6. Findings and recommendations
Finding 1. The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs) is above target and costs the service around £80,900 in clinical time every six months.
Recommendation 1. Extend reminder calls to all booked appointments, about 960 a week, using reception staff. This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost.

Finding 2. The two-DNA discharge policy is applied inconsistently.
Recommendation 2. Revise the policy to include a documented clinical review before discharge, so that vulnerable patients are protected and the policy can then be applied consistently.

Finding 3. Late-cancellation slots are refilled only 31% of the time.
Recommendation 3. Introduce an automated text offer to patients on the cancellation list when a slot becomes free.

7. Conclusion
Missed appointments are costly but largely preventable. Reminder calls have been shown to more than halve DNAs in this service, and extending them to every patient, together with the policy and process changes above, should bring the DNA rate below target within six months.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs)" -- Section 1 defines DNAs as failures to attend without notice and says late cancellations are recorded and reported separately (and section 5 reports 1,140 late cancellations 'in addition to the DNAs above'). Finding 1 says the 10.5% includes late cancellations classified as DNAs. The definition contradicts itself.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate" -- A call is only recorded as 'received' if the patient answered and confirmed attendance; unanswered calls fall into the comparison group. The groups are selected on engagement/intention to attend, and calls were made only 'where time allows', so the 6.0% vs 12.5% difference does not show the calls caused the reduction.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost." -- The document states each call takes about four minutes and staff currently make about 300 calls a week. Going to about 960 a week adds about 660 calls, roughly 44 extra staff hours a week (more than one full-time post). The memo never addresses this workload/cost although its own data raise it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy

**The document is not ready to send.** The arithmetic is correct, the structure is clear, and Recommendations 2 and 3 are sound. But the headline recommendation depends on a comparison that can't show what the memo says it shows, and its "no additional cost" claim is contradicted by the memo's own figures. Finding 1 also contradicts the Scope section. All three are fixable without new data collection.

## 1. The reminder-call comparison doesn't show that calls halve DNAs

Section 3 says a call is recorded as "received" **only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend**. Unanswered calls are not recorded. So the two groups in Table 2 are:

- **"Reminder call received" (6.0%):** patients who picked up and told staff they were coming.
- **"No reminder call recorded" (12.5%):** patients never called, *plus* everyone who was called but didn't answer, *plus* anyone who answered but didn't confirm.

The first group is selected for being reachable and intending to attend. Those patients would likely have a lower DNA rate even if the call itself did nothing. The second group contains exactly the people a reminder fails to reach.

Two further problems compound this:
- **Calls were made "where time allows,"** not at random. If staff tended to call new-patient assessments (6.6% DNA rate) more than follow-ups (11.8%), part of the gap reflects appointment type, not the call. The memo doesn't report how calls were split by type.
- **The extrapolation doesn't follow even if the effect were real.** Extending calls to everyone mainly adds patients who are harder to reach. They won't all answer, and those who don't won't get the benefit. "Would bring the service well within its 8% target" isn't supported.

This affects Section 3, Recommendation 1, and the Conclusion ("have been shown to more than halve DNAs"). The data show that **patients who confirm attendance on the phone usually attend.** That is useful, but it is not evidence that calls cause the reduction.

## 2. The "no additional cost" claim is contradicted by the memo's own figures

Using the memo's numbers:

| | Calls/week | × 4 min | Staff hours/week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current | 300 | 1,200 min | **20 h** |
| Proposed | 960 | 3,840 min | **64 h** |
| Additional | 660 | 2,640 min | **44 h** (~1.2 FTE) |

That is about 1,140 extra reception hours per six months. Calls are currently made only "where time allows," which suggests there is no slack. Absorbing 44 hours a week within existing hours needs evidence, or the claim should be removed and the cost stated. Even at modest reception pay rates this is a material sum against the £80,900 figure, especially since the size of the true benefit is unknown (see point 1).

The author's summary also says "it does not need new funding." That is the claim most likely to be challenged by an operations director.

## 3. Finding 1 contradicts the rest of the memo

Finding 1 says the 10.5% rate is "including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs." But:
- The Scope says late cancellations are "recorded and reported separately."
- Section 5 says the 1,140 late cancellations are "in addition to the DNAs above."
- 2,610 / 24,860 = 10.5%. Adding the late cancellations would give 3,750 / 24,860 = **15.1%**.

This looks like a drafting error, but it undermines the definitional care the memo is otherwise proud of. Delete the parenthetical.

## 4. Smaller points

- **"Costs the service £80,900":** this is the value of unused clinical time, not a cash cost. Clinicians are paid regardless. Phrase it as "the equivalent of around £80,900 of clinical time" (as Section 2 already does) so it isn't read as a recoverable saving.
- **Completeness ≠ causation.** The author's note says that because the full record was used, "the rates are exact." That is true of the descriptive rates. It doesn't help with the selection problem in point 1, so the memo shouldn't imply it does.
- **Text reminders.** Recommendation 3 already proposes automated texts for the cancellation list. The obvious question is whether automated text reminders would be a cheaper alternative to 64 hours a week of calls. It's worth a sentence.
- Recommendations 2 and 3 are proportionate and well supported. Discharge was applied in 104 of 160 cases (65%), and only 31% of about 1,140 late-cancellation slots were refilled.

## Suggested revision to make it decision-ready

1. **Reword Section 3** to describe what the data show: confirmed patients DNA at 6.0%, everyone else at 12.5%, and the difference can't be attributed to the call because only answered-and-confirmed calls are recorded.
2. **Replace Recommendation 1** with a time-limited test. For example, extend calls (or trial SMS reminders) at one site, or in alternating weeks, for 8–12 weeks. Record **every** call attempt and outcome (answered, unanswered, rescheduled), and compare DNA rates against a comparable period or site. This gives the Division a real effect size before committing staff time.
3. **State the staffing cost** of full roll-out (about 64 h/week, 44 h above current), or show how it can be absorbed.
4. **Delete the parenthetical in Finding 1.**
5. **Soften the Conclusion**: e.g. "Reminders are a promising, low-cost intervention; we recommend testing them properly before full roll-out, alongside the policy and process changes above."

With those changes, the memo would give the Director a clear, defensible recommendation. In its current form, the central claim is likely to be challenged and could lead to staff time being committed on the basis of an overstated effect.
